title: Energy Efficiency and Fairness of Local Large Language Models in Data Stream Processing.
abstract: Data stream processing aims to provide real-time insights and has use cases in sensitive domains such as finance and healthcare, where algorithmic fairness is a critical concern. As resource-constrained environments are common deployment choices for stream processing, energy efficiency is also crucial. This study investigates the viability of LLMs for data stream processing, focusing on three key aspects: energy efficiency, fairness, and performance-wise feasibility. We implemented an LLM-based data stream processing system and systematically evaluated multiple LLMs against traditional ML approaches in a real-time credit card fraud detection use case. Our empirical analysis reveals significant disparities in energy efficiency: traditional ML models consume 2.6-2.7 kJ, while LLMs require 117.9-1064.2 kJ for equivalent processing. Although LLMs demonstrated more balanced treatment across demographic groups, with a disparate impact ratio between 0.95 and 1.05, compared to traditional models’ range of 0.4 to 2.0, they exhibited lower fraud-detection performance than conventional approaches. GPU utilization patterns indicate that LLMs require substantial computational resources, with 62.6-83.8% of energy consumption attributed to GPU operations. The further analysis revealed varying degrees of reliability, with hallucination rates ranging from 13.6% to 53.4% across LLMs. Our findings suggest that while LLMs could help reduce algorithmic bias, their energy consumption may limit their use in data stream processing.
